title: Comparative Advantage and Trade Policy
bigQuestion: If trade between countries makes both sides richer on average, why do so many people argue about it?

story.title: One Ship, Two Directions
story.kicker: A container ship leaves a Pacific port full of phones and comes back with beans that grew in Illinois dirt.
paragraphs: In October a truck pulls out of a farm near Bloomington, Illinois, loaded with soybeans that were in the ground in April. It drives to a river elevator on the Illinois River, where the beans pour into a barge. The barge floats down to the Mississippi and on to a port near New Orleans. There a crane lifts the beans into the hold of a ship bound for Asia. Most of the soybeans grown in Illinois never become an Illinois meal. They become animal feed and cooking oil on the far side of the world.

The same ship, a few weeks earlier, came the other way. Its containers held phones, laptops, televisions and the small parts that go into cars built in Michigan and Illinois. A store in Naperville sold one of those phones to a student who paid for it with money from a summer job. She never thought about the ship. She thought about the price.

Look at a manifest, the list of everything a ship carries, and you are looking at a set of choices. Somebody in Illinois decided that growing soybeans paid better than trying to build phones. Somebody in a factory across the ocean decided the reverse. Nobody ordered them to do it. Each side looked at what it could do well, what it could do cheaply, and what the other side would pay.

Trade like this makes both sides richer on average, and economists have understood why for two hundred years. But the average hides a lot. The soybean farmer gains. The phone buyer gains. A worker whose factory closed because a rival overseas made the same product for less does not gain, at least not soon. That is why nearly every country taxes some imports, and why trade is one of the most argued-about subjects in economics.

This chapter follows the ship both ways. First it asks why two countries trade at all, even when one of them is better at making everything. Then it counts the flow, asks what a trade deficit actually means, and looks at the tools governments use to slow trade down. Along the way it keeps asking the one question that matters most: who pays, and who gains?
story.think: The student in Naperville and the farmer near Bloomington never met. In what sense did they trade with each other?

lessons.title: Absolute Advantage
lessons.mainIdea: A producer has an absolute advantage when it can make more of a good with the same resources than another producer can.
reading: Imagine two small countries, Aland and Bland, that each make only two things: shirts and wheat. In one hour of work, a worker in Aland can sew 4 shirts or grow 2 bushels of wheat. In one hour, a worker in Bland can sew 1 shirt or grow 1 bushel of wheat. Aland's workers make more shirts per hour and more wheat per hour. Economists say Aland has an *absolute advantage* in both goods.

An absolute advantage means you can produce more of something than someone else using the same amount of a *resource*, such as an hour of labor or an acre of land. It is the most natural way to compare producers, and it is the way Adam Smith described trade in 1776. If your neighbor bakes better bread and you fix better bicycles, you each do what you do best and swap. Both of you end up with better bread and a working bike.

But this leaves a puzzle. In our example Aland is better at both things. If absolute advantage were the whole story, Aland would have no reason to trade with Bland at all. It could just make everything itself. Yet countries in exactly this position trade with each other all the time. The United States, with some of the most productive workers in the world, imports goods from countries with far less productive workers.

The answer to the puzzle is the subject of the next lesson. For now, get the first idea straight. Absolute advantage answers the question, who can make more? It does not answer the question, who should make what? To answer that one, we have to look at what each producer gives up, which is the idea of opportunity cost you already know.

words.d: being able to make more of a good than another producer with the same amount of resources
anything used to produce goods and services, such as an hour of labor, a machine or an acre of land
how much output a worker or a machine produces in a given amount of time

look.title: Output Per Hour in Two Countries (Example)
rows: Aland: bushels of wheat per hour
Bland: bushels of wheat per hour
look.prompt: Which country has the absolute advantage in shirts? In wheat? How many times more productive is Aland in each good?

check.q: In the example, why does Aland have an absolute advantage in wheat?
choices: Its workers grow more bushels per hour than Bland's workers
Its wheat sells for a higher price
It gives up fewer shirts to grow wheat
It has more workers than Bland
check.why: Absolute advantage compares output per unit of resource. Aland grows 2 bushels an hour; Bland grows 1.

check.q: A worker in Country X builds 6 chairs an hour; a worker in Country Y builds 9. Who has the absolute advantage in chairs?
choices: Country X
Country Y
Neither, since both build chairs
It depends on the price of chairs
check.why: Country Y makes more chairs with the same hour of labor, so it has the absolute advantage.

check.q: What puzzle does absolute advantage fail to explain?
choices: Why workers in different countries earn different wages
Why some countries have more land than others
Why a country that is better at everything still trades
Why prices rise when demand rises
check.why: Aland is better at both goods yet countries like it still trade. Absolute advantage alone cannot say why.

lessons.title: Comparative Advantage
lessons.mainIdea: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lowest opportunity cost, and that is what decides who should make what.
reading: Go back to Aland and Bland and ask a different question. Not who can make more, but who gives up less. In Aland, an hour spent growing 2 bushels of wheat is an hour not spent sewing 4 shirts. So each bushel of wheat costs Aland 2 shirts. In Bland, an hour growing 1 bushel is an hour not sewing 1 shirt. Each bushel of wheat costs Bland only 1 shirt. Bland gives up less to grow wheat.

Now flip it. Each shirt costs Aland half a bushel of wheat, since 4 shirts equal 2 bushels. Each shirt costs Bland a full bushel. So Aland gives up less to make shirts. The country with the lower *opportunity cost* for a good has the *comparative advantage* in that good. Bland has the comparative advantage in wheat. Aland has the comparative advantage in shirts, even though Aland is better at both in absolute terms.

This is the idea David Ricardo worked out in 1817, and it is one of the few results in economics that almost every economist accepts. A country cannot have a comparative advantage in everything, because opportunity costs are ratios. If Aland gives up fewer shirts per bushel, it must give up more bushels per shirt. Somebody always has the lower cost in each good, so there is always a basis for trade.

The common mistake is to compare raw output and stop there. Students see that Aland makes more of both and conclude Aland should make everything. Check yourself by computing the opportunity cost of each good in each country, as a ratio, and then compare the ratios. The lower ratio wins that good. A country should *specialize* in what it does at the lowest cost to itself, not in what it does best compared with others.

words.d: being able to make a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer
the next-best thing you give up when you make a choice
to concentrate on producing one good or a few goods instead of trying to make everything

look.title: The Lawyer Who Types Fast
look.text: A lawyer bills $300 an hour and can type 90 words a minute. Her assistant types 60 words a minute and earns $25 an hour. The lawyer has the absolute advantage in typing. Yet she hands the typing to the assistant. Work out what one hour of typing costs the lawyer and what it costs the assistant, in dollars of other work not done.
look.prompt: Who has the comparative advantage in typing, and why does the lawyer's faster typing not change the answer?

check.q: In one hour, Country P makes 10 phones or 5 bikes. What is P's opportunity cost of one bike?
choices: 5 phones
10 phones
Half a phone
2 phones
check.why: 5 bikes cost 10 phones, so one bike costs 10 divided by 5, which is 2 phones.

check.q: Country P gives up 2 phones per bike; Country Q gives up 3 phones per bike. Who has the comparative advantage in bikes?
choices: Country P, because its opportunity cost per bike is lower
Country Q, because it gives up more
Neither, because both make bikes
Whichever makes more bikes per hour
check.why: Comparative advantage goes to the lower opportunity cost. P gives up only 2 phones per bike.

check.q: Why can a country not have a comparative advantage in every good?
choices: Because every country has the same workers
Because opportunity costs are ratios, so a low cost in one good means a high cost in the other
Because governments forbid it
Because absolute advantage prevents it
check.why: If you give up fewer shirts per bushel, you must give up more bushels per shirt. The ratios flip.

lessons.title: Gains From Trade
lessons.mainIdea: When each country specializes in its comparative advantage and trades, both end up with more than they could make alone.
reading: Let us prove the gain with numbers. Suppose a worker in each country has an 8-hour day. Without trade, each splits the day. The Aland worker spends 4 hours on shirts and 4 on wheat: 16 shirts and 8 bushels. The Bland worker does the same: 4 shirts and 4 bushels. Together the two workers produce 20 shirts and 12 bushels. That is the total the world gets when each country tries to make both things.

Now let them specialize by comparative advantage. Bland spends all 8 hours on wheat and grows 8 bushels. Aland shifts toward shirts: 6 hours on shirts makes 24, and 2 hours on wheat makes 4 bushels. Together they now have 24 shirts and 12 bushels. The same two workers, the same day, and 4 more shirts with no less wheat. Nothing was invented. The gain came only from putting each hour where it cost the least.

Trade shares the gain. They agree on *terms of trade* of 1.5 shirts per bushel, which lies between the two opportunity costs of 1 and 2. Bland sends Aland 4 bushels and gets 6 shirts back. Bland ends the day with 4 bushels and 6 shirts, instead of 4 and 4. Aland ends with 18 shirts and 8 bushels, instead of 16 and 8. Both countries have more of at least one good and no less of the other. That is the *gains from trade*.

Notice why the price mattered. If Aland had demanded 2 shirts per bushel, Bland would be no better off than growing shirts itself, so it would refuse. If Bland demanded 1 shirt per bushel, Aland would refuse. Any price between the two opportunity costs leaves both better off. In the real world millions of prices are set this way, in markets, and the same logic explains why an Illinois farmer sells soybeans abroad and buys a phone made overseas.

words.d: the extra goods and services both sides get when they specialize and trade instead of making everything themselves
the rate at which one good is exchanged for another between trading partners
focusing production on the goods a producer makes at the lowest opportunity cost

look.title: Adam Smith on Buying Instead of Making
look.text: It is the maxim of every prudent master of a family, never to attempt to make at home what it will cost him more to make than to buy.
look.cite: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book IV, 1776
look.prompt: Smith goes on to say that what is prudent for a family can scarcely be foolish for a whole kingdom. Restate his point using the words opportunity cost.

check.q: In the example, how many more shirts did the world get after specialization, with no loss of wheat?
choices: 12 more shirts
8 more shirts
4 more shirts
None; the total stayed at 20
check.why: Total shirts rose from 20 to 24 while wheat stayed at 12 bushels. That is 4 extra shirts.

check.q: Why must the terms of trade lie between 1 and 2 shirts per bushel in the example?
choices: Because prices must always be whole numbers
Because that is the only range in which both countries gain
Because the government sets the price at 1.5
Because Aland has the absolute advantage
check.why: At 2 shirts per bushel Bland gains nothing; at 1 shirt Aland gains nothing. In between, both do better than going alone.

check.q: After trading 4 bushels for 6 shirts, how many shirts and bushels does Bland have?
choices: 4 shirts and 4 bushels
8 shirts and 0 bushels
6 shirts and 8 bushels
6 shirts and 4 bushels
check.why: Bland grew 8 bushels, sent 4 away and received 6 shirts, leaving 6 shirts and 4 bushels.

lessons.title: Exports, Imports and the Balance
lessons.mainIdea: Exports are goods and services sold to other countries, imports are those bought from them, and the trade balance is exports minus imports.
reading: An *export* is anything made in one country and sold to a buyer in another. Illinois soybeans on a ship to Asia are exports. So is a Chicago software company's subscription sold to a firm in Germany, because services count too. An *import* is the reverse: anything made abroad and bought here. The phone in Naperville, a car built in Mexico and a vacation a Chicago family takes in Italy are all imports.

The *trade balance* is simply exports minus imports for a country over a period, usually a year. Suppose in an example year a country exports $2,000 billion of goods and services and imports $2,500 billion. Its trade balance is $2,000 billion minus $2,500 billion, or negative $500 billion. A negative balance is called a *trade deficit*. If exports had been larger than imports, the positive balance would be a *trade surplus*.

The United States has run a trade deficit every year for roughly fifty years. It sells enormous amounts abroad, but it buys even more. Illinois follows a similar pattern in goods, exporting farm products, machinery and chemicals while importing electronics, vehicles and oil. Because the numbers are so big, news reports usually give them in billions and compare them to the size of the whole economy.

One habit worth building: check which direction the money flows. When an Illinois farmer sells soybeans to a buyer in Japan, the beans go out and dollars come in. When a Chicago store buys phones from a factory in Vietnam, phones come in and dollars go out. Exports bring money in; imports send it out. The trade balance is the net result, and a deficit means more money went out for goods and services than came in.

words.d: a good or service produced in one country and sold to a buyer in another country
a good or service produced abroad and bought by people or businesses in this country
a country's exports minus its imports over a period of time
a negative trade balance; imports are larger than exports
a positive trade balance; exports are larger than imports

look.title: One Country's Trade in a Year (Example)
look.prompt: Add up total exports and total imports. What is the trade balance? Is it a deficit or a surplus, and is the balance in services alone positive or negative?

check.q: A country exports $800 billion and imports $950 billion. What is its trade balance?
choices: A surplus of $150 billion
A deficit of $150 billion
A surplus of $1,750 billion
A deficit of $950 billion
check.why: Exports minus imports is $800 billion minus $950 billion, or negative $150 billion, a deficit.

check.q: A family from Chicago spends a week at hotels in Spain. For the United States, that spending counts as
choices: an export of services
an import of goods
an import of services
neither, because no goods crossed a border
check.why: The family bought a service produced abroad, so it is an import of services.

check.q: Which flow brings money into a country?
choices: Imports of goods
Imports of services
A trade deficit
Exports
check.why: When a country sells exports, foreign buyers pay for them, so money flows in.

lessons.title: What a Trade Deficit Means
lessons.mainIdea: A trade deficit means a country buys more from abroad than it sells, and the difference is matched by foreign investment flowing in; it is not a scoreboard of winning or losing.
reading: People often hear the word deficit and assume it means loss, like a business losing money. A trade deficit is not that. When an American buys a $600 phone from a factory abroad, the American gets a phone worth $600 to her and the factory gets $600. Nobody lost. The deficit records only that, added up across the whole country, Americans bought more goods and services from foreigners than foreigners bought from Americans.

So where do the extra dollars go? A foreign factory that earns dollars can spend them on American goods, which would be an export. Or it can invest them in America by buying a Treasury bond, shares of an American company or a warehouse in Joliet. Every dollar that leaves for an import comes back one way or the other. A trade deficit in goods and services is matched by a surplus in *capital flows*: foreigners investing more in the United States than Americans invest abroad.

This is why economists are split about whether a trade deficit is a problem. On one side: it means foreigners are lending to us and buying our assets, and that borrowing has to be paid back with interest someday. A deficit can also fall hardest on particular industries and towns. On the other side: the investment builds factories and funds the government, and a country whose people and firms are attractive to invest in will naturally run a deficit. Both sides agree the deficit alone does not tell you whether a country is doing well.

Watch for two common mistakes. First, a trade deficit is not the same as the *federal budget deficit*, which is government spending minus tax revenue. They are different numbers about different things, even though both use the word deficit. Second, a deficit with one country means little on its own. The United States can run a deficit with one trading partner, a surplus with another, and the overall balance is what economists study.

words.d: money moving between countries to buy assets such as bonds, stocks, factories and buildings
the amount by which the federal government's spending exceeds its tax revenue in a year
anything of value that can be owned, such as a bond, a share of stock or a building

look.title: Your Own Trade Deficit
look.text: You run a trade deficit with your grocery store every week: you buy from it and it buys nothing from you. You run a trade surplus with your employer, who buys your labor and sells you nothing. Overall, your imports and exports roughly balance, or you borrow. Now imagine a whole country whose people buy more from abroad than they sell, year after year, while foreigners buy its bonds and build factories inside it.
look.prompt: Using the household picture, explain why a deficit with one partner is not by itself a sign of trouble, and what would be a sign of trouble.

check.q: When Americans buy more from abroad than they sell, what happens to the extra dollars foreigners earn?
choices: They disappear from the economy
They are invested in American assets or lent to Americans
They are destroyed by the Federal Reserve
They must be returned as gifts
check.why: Dollars earned abroad come back as investment in American bonds, stocks, land and businesses.

check.q: Which statement about a trade deficit is correct?
choices: It is the same thing as the federal budget deficit
It proves a country is losing money
It means imports exceeded exports over the period
It means one country cheated another
check.why: A trade deficit is simply imports larger than exports. It is a different number from the budget deficit.

check.q: Which is a reasonable worry about a long-running trade deficit?
choices: Foreign lending has to be repaid with interest someday
It means no Americans have jobs
It means the country exports nothing
It always causes inflation
check.why: A deficit is matched by foreign investment and lending, and lending must be repaid. The other statements are false.

lessons.title: Illinois in the World Market
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois sells farm products, machinery and chemicals to the world and depends on rivers, rails and ports to do it.
reading: Illinois is one of the biggest exporting states in the country, and its exports show comparative advantage at work. The state has some of the richest farmland on Earth, so it is regularly among the top two states for soybeans and corn. It has a long history of building heavy machinery, from construction equipment to farm tractors. And it has chemical and pharmaceutical plants. These are the goods that Illinois can make at a lower opportunity cost than most of the world.

Geography matters too. The Illinois River flows into the Mississippi, which carries barges to the Gulf of Mexico. Chicago is the busiest rail hub in North America, where lines from both coasts meet. O'Hare handles enormous amounts of air cargo. Because moving goods is cheaper here than in many places, businesses that need to ship things choose Illinois, and that in turn strengthens its advantage.

Illinois's largest trading partners are its neighbors. Canada and Mexico buy more from Illinois than any other countries, which is why trade agreements with them matter so much to the state. Trucks and trains cross those borders every day carrying machinery, parts and food. Farther away, buyers in Asia take a large share of the state's soybeans, and Europe buys chemicals and medicines.

Trade cuts the other way as well. When another country puts a *tariff*, a tax on imports, on American soybeans, Illinois farmers feel it first, because the buyers turn to soybeans from Brazil instead. When the price of imported steel rises, Illinois machinery makers pay more for their inputs. A state that sells so much to the world is also one of the states most exposed to what happens when trade slows. That exposure is the reason Illinois politicians of every stripe watch trade policy closely.

words.d: a tax a government charges on goods imported from other countries
a good or service used to produce something else, such as steel used to build a tractor
a country that buys from and sells to another country

look.title: A Barge on the Illinois River
look.text: One barge on the Illinois River can carry roughly as much grain as 15 rail cars or about 60 trucks, and it costs far less per ton to move. Picture a farmer near Peoria choosing between selling soybeans to a local buyer for $11 a bushel and shipping them to a river elevator that pays $11.60 but charges $0.35 a bushel to haul and load.
look.prompt: Which choice pays more per bushel, and by how much? How does cheap river transport help explain why Illinois exports so many soybeans?

check.q: Which best explains why Illinois exports so many soybeans?
choices: Illinois has a law requiring farmers to export
Rich soil and cheap transport give it a low opportunity cost in soybeans
Soybeans cannot be grown anywhere else
Illinois imports no food
check.why: Comparative advantage comes from low opportunity cost, and Illinois's soil and rivers give it that in soybeans.

check.q: If another country puts a tariff on U.S. soybeans, what is the most likely first effect in Illinois?
choices: Illinois soybean prices rise sharply
Illinois farmers plant more soybeans
Foreign buyers turn to other suppliers, and Illinois farmers sell less or for less
Chicago's rail traffic doubles
check.why: A tariff raises the price of U.S. soybeans abroad, so buyers switch to suppliers such as Brazil.

check.q: Which countries are Illinois's largest trading partners?
choices: Japan and Germany
Brazil and Argentina
France and Italy
Canada and Mexico
check.why: Illinois's neighbors to the north and south buy more from the state than any other countries.

lessons.title: How a Tariff Works
lessons.mainIdea: A tariff raises the price of imports, which helps domestic producers and the treasury but costs consumers more than those two gain.
reading: A tariff is a tax on an imported good, collected at the border. Suppose an imported bicycle sells for $200 and the government sets a 25% tariff. The importer must pay $50 in tax, so the bike now costs $250 to bring in and the store price rises toward $250. American bike makers who were losing sales at $200 can now sell at close to $250 too. That is the point of a *protective tariff*: it protects domestic producers from foreign competition.

Trace who gains and who pays. Consumers pay: everyone who buys a bike, imported or not, pays up to $50 more, and some people who would have bought at $200 do not buy at all. The government gains: it collects $50 on every imported bike that still comes in. Domestic producers gain: they sell more bikes at a higher price. When economists add up all three, the loss to consumers is bigger than the gain to the treasury plus the gain to producers. The difference is called the *deadweight loss* of the tariff.

Why is the loss bigger? Because the tariff causes two kinds of waste. Some bikes are now built at home for $240 that could have been bought abroad for $200, using up $40 of resources for nothing. And some people who valued a bike at $220 no longer buy one, losing a deal that would have made them better off. Neither of those losses shows up as anyone's gain.

The question of who really pays a tariff is the same *tax incidence* question you met with sales taxes. The importer writes the check, but it passes most of the cost to the buyer through a higher price. How much passes through depends on elasticity. If buyers have few substitutes, they absorb nearly all of it. If the foreign seller badly needs the American market, it may cut its price and absorb some. In most studied cases, most of a tariff lands on the buyers in the country that imposed it.

words.d: a tariff meant mainly to shield domestic producers from foreign competition rather than to raise revenue
value lost to society when a tax or control prevents trades that would have made both sides better off
who actually bears the cost of a tax, regardless of who writes the check
how strongly the quantity demanded or supplied responds to a change in price

look.title: Bicycle Market With and Without a Tariff (Example)
rows: World price of an imported bike
Price in the store after the tariff
look.prompt: How many fewer bikes are sold after the tariff? If 50 thousand of the 80 thousand are still imported, how much revenue does the government collect?

check.q: An imported jacket costs $80 and faces a 15% tariff. What is the tariff per jacket?
check.why: 15% of $80 is 0.15 times 80, which is $12.

check.q: Who is most likely to end up paying most of a tariff on imported goods?
choices: The foreign government
Buyers in the country that imposed it, through higher prices
The shipping company
Domestic producers of the same good
check.why: The importer passes most of the tax on through a higher price, so domestic buyers bear most of it.

check.q: Why does a tariff create a deadweight loss?
choices: Because the government spends the revenue
Because foreign producers earn more
Because the treasury collects too much
Because some resources are wasted making goods at home that were cheaper abroad, and some good deals never happen
check.why: The loss to consumers exceeds the producer and treasury gains because of wasted resources and lost trades.

lessons.title: Quotas and Other Barriers
lessons.mainIdea: A quota limits the quantity imported instead of taxing it, raising the price like a tariff but sending the extra money to whoever holds the import rights.
reading: A *quota* is a legal limit on how much of a good may be imported in a period. Instead of taxing each bike, the government might say: only 50,000 imported bikes this year. If Americans wanted 100,000 imported bikes at the world price of $200, the quota creates a shortage of imports. The price rises until buyers want only what is allowed, plus whatever domestic makers add. In our example the price might settle near $250, the same as under the tariff.

The difference is where the extra $50 per bike goes. Under a tariff, the government collects it. Under a quota, the firm that holds the right to import collects it, because it buys at $200 abroad and sells at $250 here. Those import rights become valuable, and if they go to foreign sellers, the money leaves the country entirely. This is why most economists, if forced to choose, prefer a tariff to a quota of the same size: at least the revenue stays home.

Countries also slow trade in quieter ways. A *voluntary export restraint* is a quota in disguise: one country agrees to limit its own exports so the other will not impose a tariff. Safety, health and labeling rules can be genuine protections or can be written to keep out foreign goods. Subsidies to domestic producers let them undercut imports. Long customs delays act like a tax on time. Together these are called *non-tariff barriers*, and they are often harder to see and argue about than a tariff rate.

The economic effect of every barrier is the same in direction. Prices rise for consumers, domestic producers sell more, the quantity traded falls, and some value is lost. The barriers differ in who captures the price increase and in how visible they are. When you read about a trade dispute, ask two questions: what tool is being used, and who gets the extra money?

words.d: a legal limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported during a period
an agreement by one country to limit its exports to another, usually to avoid a tariff
any rule other than a tariff that makes importing harder, such as a quota, a licensing requirement or a customs delay
a payment from the government to a producer that lowers the producer's cost

look.title: Sugar Above the World Price
look.text: For decades the United States has limited sugar imports with quotas, so the price of sugar inside the country has often been well above the world price. Candy makers, some of them in Chicago, pay more for sugar, while American sugar growers get a higher price. A few candy factories have moved operations to Canada or Mexico, where sugar is cheaper.
look.prompt: List who gains and who loses from the sugar quota. Why might the losers, who are far more numerous, have less political influence than the winners?

check.q: What is the main difference between a tariff and a quota of the same size?
choices: A quota lowers prices while a tariff raises them
Under a quota the price increase goes to import-right holders, not to the government
A tariff limits quantity while a quota does not affect it
A quota only applies to services
check.why: Both raise the domestic price, but only the tariff sends the extra money to the treasury.

check.q: A country agrees to limit its own car exports to avoid a tariff. This is called
choices: a voluntary export restraint
a subsidy
a trade surplus
free trade
check.why: A voluntary export restraint is a self-imposed export limit adopted to head off a tariff.

check.q: Which of these is a non-tariff barrier?
choices: A 10% tax on imported steel
A price ceiling on gasoline
An inspection rule designed so that foreign fruit rarely passes
A cut in the income tax
check.why: A rule written to keep out foreign goods without taxing them is a non-tariff barrier.

lessons.title: The Case for Protection
lessons.mainIdea: Supporters of trade barriers argue they protect new industries, national security and jobs, and some of these arguments have real weight in particular cases.
reading: If trade barriers cost consumers more than they gain producers, why does nearly every country use them? Serious arguments exist, and a fair student should know them. The oldest is the *infant industry* argument. A new industry in a country may not be able to compete yet with established foreign firms. Protect it for a while, the argument goes, and it will grow, learn and eventually stand alone. Several countries that industrialized quickly, including the United States in the 1800s, used tariffs in this way.

A second argument is national security. A country may not want to depend on a rival for steel, computer chips, medicine or food, even if imports are cheaper. If a war or a crisis cut off the supply, the cheapness would not matter. Most economists accept that this argument justifies some protection for a narrow set of truly essential goods. The disagreement is about how wide that set really is, since almost every industry claims to be essential.

The most common argument is jobs. When a factory closes because imports undercut it, the workers, their families and their town lose. Economic theory says the gains from trade are large enough that the winners could compensate the losers. In practice that compensation is often small and late. A worker who spent twenty years making furniture cannot easily become a software engineer at fifty. Protection that slows the change gives towns time to adjust. Critics answer that it also freezes resources in industries where they no longer belong.

There are two more arguments you will hear. One is fairness: if another country subsidizes its exporters or blocks our goods, our barriers are a response, and the threat of them is a bargaining tool. The other is that trade can be used to pressure countries over human rights or environmental damage. Each of these has some force. Each is also easy to abuse by an industry that simply wants less competition. The economic way to judge them is to ask what the barrier costs consumers and whether a cheaper tool would reach the same goal.

words.d: a new industry that supporters say needs temporary protection until it can compete with established foreign firms
the policy of using tariffs, quotas and other barriers to shield domestic producers from imports
the process by which workers and businesses move out of shrinking industries and into growing ones

look.title: A Chip Factory or Cheaper Chips
look.text: A country can import computer chips for $10 each or protect a new domestic chip factory whose chips cost $14 to make. Every device maker in the country would pay the extra $4. Supporters say the factory will get cheaper with experience and that chips are too important to rely on one foreign supplier. Opponents say the factory may never catch up and that phones and cars will cost more for everyone.
look.prompt: Write the strongest version of each side's case. What fact, if you could learn it, would most change your mind?

check.q: The infant industry argument says a tariff should be
choices: permanent, to keep prices high
applied only to farm goods
temporary, until a new industry can compete on its own
used only against wealthy countries
check.why: The argument rests on the industry growing up. Protection is supposed to end once it can compete.

check.q: Which argument for protection do most economists accept for at least a narrow set of goods?
choices: That imports always cost jobs overall
That the country should make everything itself
That tariffs lower prices for consumers
That a country should not depend on rivals for truly essential goods
check.why: National security justifies some protection for essentials; the debate is over how many goods really qualify.

check.q: Why is the jobs argument for protection powerful even if total gains from trade are large?
choices: Because the losses fall hard on specific workers and towns and compensation is often small
Because trade creates no jobs anywhere
Because consumers never gain from imports
Because factories cannot be built without tariffs
check.why: Gains are spread thin across millions of consumers while losses concentrate on a few, who are rarely fully compensated.

lessons.title: The Case Against Protection
lessons.mainIdea: Opponents of trade barriers point to higher prices for consumers, costs to industries that use imports, retaliation by other countries and the history of tariff wars.
reading: Start with the arithmetic from the tariff lesson: consumers lose more than producers and the treasury gain. Studies of real tariffs regularly find that each job protected costs consumers far more than that job pays. A tariff that saves a $50,000 factory job by raising prices $200,000 across the country is a bad trade even for the workers, since the same money could retrain three of them and still leave the country ahead. Economists call this the *cost per job saved*, and it is usually startling.

Second, most imports are not finished goods for shoppers. They are *intermediate goods*: steel for tractors, parts for cars, chemicals for medicines. A tariff on steel helps steel mills but hurts every factory that uses steel, and those factories employ many more people than the mills do. Illinois machinery makers are a clear case. Protect one link in the chain and you tax all the links after it.

Third is *retaliation*. When one country raises tariffs, its trading partners usually answer with tariffs of their own, aimed at the first country's most politically sensitive exports. American farm goods, including Illinois soybeans, are a frequent target. The Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 raised American tariffs sharply during the early Great Depression. Other countries retaliated, world trade shrank, and most economists believe the tariff made the Depression worse, even if it did not cause it.

The honest summary is that economists broadly favor open trade while agreeing that it has real losers who deserve real help. The disagreement in public life is about how much weight to give the losers, how much to trust the arguments for exceptions, and whether help for displaced workers will actually arrive. Those are partly questions of values, not just economics. What economics can do is put numbers on the costs so that the choice is made with open eyes.

words.d: the total extra amount consumers pay because of a trade barrier, divided by the number of jobs the barrier protects
a good used as an input to make another good, such as steel used to build machinery
a country's answer to another country's trade barriers with barriers of its own

look.title: Bastiat's Petition of the Candlemakers
look.text: In 1845 the French economist Frederic Bastiat wrote a mock petition from candlemakers to the French legislature. They complained of ruinous competition from a foreign rival who flooded the market with light at no price at all: the sun. They asked for a law requiring every window and shutter to be closed, which would boost demand for candles and, they claimed, every industry that supplied candlemakers.
look.cite: Frederic Bastiat, Petition of the Candlemakers, 1845 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Bastiat was making fun of a real argument. Which argument for protection was he attacking, and why does the joke work?

check.q: A tariff protects 1,000 jobs and raises consumer costs by $300 million a year. What is the cost per job saved?
check.why: $300,000,000 divided by 1,000 jobs is $300,000 per job.

check.q: Why can a tariff on steel cost more jobs than it saves?
choices: Because steel is not used in anything else
Because industries that use steel as an input employ far more people than steel mills
Because steel mills refuse to hire
Because the tariff lowers the price of steel
check.why: Steel is an intermediate good. Raising its price hurts every downstream manufacturer.

check.q: What happened after the United States raised tariffs sharply in 1930?
choices: World trade grew quickly
Other countries lowered their tariffs in response
Prices fell for American consumers
Other countries retaliated and world trade shrank
check.why: Trading partners answered Smoot-Hawley with their own tariffs, and world trade fell sharply.

lessons.title: Trade Agreements
lessons.mainIdea: Trade agreements are treaties in which countries lower barriers together, so each side gets market access in exchange for giving it.
reading: A country could lower its tariffs alone, and economists say it would gain from doing so. Politically that is hard, because the losers are visible and the winners are scattered. A *trade agreement* solves part of the problem. Two or more countries agree to cut barriers at the same time. Now the deal has visible winners at home, the exporters who gain access to foreign markets, and they push for it as hard as protected industries push against it.

The most important agreement for Illinois is the one with Canada and Mexico. The North American Free Trade Agreement took effect in 1994 and removed most tariffs among the three countries. It was replaced in 2020 by the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which kept most of the structure and added new rules for cars, digital trade and labor. Because Canada and Mexico are Illinois's biggest customers, changes to these agreements matter more in Illinois than in most states.

A *free trade area* removes tariffs among members but lets each keep its own tariffs on outsiders. A *customs union* goes further and sets one common tariff for everyone outside. A common market adds free movement of workers and money. The European Union is the largest example of the deeper kind. Each step gives up more national control in exchange for more integration, which is why each step is also more controversial.

Agreements always contain compromises. A deal that opens markets for Illinois machinery may also open American markets to foreign farm goods, and the affected farmers object. Rules about where a product must be made to count as domestic, called rules of origin, fill hundreds of pages. Judge an agreement the way you judge a tariff: who gets more market access, who faces more competition, and what happens to the prices consumers pay.

words.d: a treaty in which two or more countries agree to lower trade barriers among themselves
a group of countries that remove tariffs among themselves while keeping their own tariffs on outsiders
a group of countries that remove tariffs among themselves and share one common tariff on outsiders
the rules in a trade agreement that decide whether a product counts as made inside the agreement area

look.title: A Tractor Built in Three Countries
look.text: An Illinois factory assembles a tractor using an engine from Mexico, electronics from Canada and steel from a country outside North America. Under the agreement, the tractor crosses the Canadian border tariff-free only if enough of its value was created inside the three member countries. If not, it faces Canada's regular tariff.
look.prompt: Why would an agreement need rules of origin at all? What might the factory do if its tractor falls just short of the required share?

check.q: Why are trade agreements often easier to pass than one-sided tariff cuts?
choices: Because agreements raise tariffs on everyone
Because they give exporters a visible gain at home to fight for
Because consumers do not notice them
Because they require no vote
check.why: An agreement creates visible winners, exporters who gain access abroad, who balance the protected industries.

check.q: Which agreement currently governs trade between the United States, Canada and Mexico?
choices: The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement
The European Union
The Smoot-Hawley Tariff
The Bretton Woods agreement
check.why: The USMCA replaced NAFTA in 2020.

check.q: What makes a customs union different from a free trade area?
choices: A customs union keeps tariffs among members
A customs union bans all imports
A customs union covers services only
Members of a customs union share one common tariff on outsiders
check.why: In a free trade area each member sets its own outside tariff; in a customs union they share one.

lessons.title: The World Trade Organization
lessons.mainIdea: The WTO is the forum where most countries set shared trade rules and settle disputes, with real influence but limited power to enforce.
reading: After the tariff wars of the 1930s and the Second World War, countries wanted rules to keep trade from collapsing again. In 1947 a group of them signed the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, or GATT, and spent the next decades negotiating round after round of tariff cuts. In 1995 the GATT became a permanent organization, the *World Trade Organization*, based in Geneva. Today more than 160 countries belong, and together they carry out nearly all world trade. China joined in 2001, a change that reshaped global manufacturing.

The WTO rests on a few core rules. The most important is *most-favored-nation* treatment: a member must offer every other member the lowest tariff it offers to any of them, with exceptions for free trade areas. Another is national treatment: once a foreign good has cleared customs, it must be treated like a domestic good. Members bind their tariffs, promising not to raise them above agreed ceilings without compensating others.

When one member believes another has broken the rules, it can bring a dispute. Panels of trade experts hear both sides and issue a ruling. If the losing country does not comply, the winner may impose retaliatory tariffs of an approved size. The WTO has no police and cannot force anyone; its power comes from the fact that members want the rules to hold for everyone else. In recent years its dispute system has weakened as some large members have blocked appointments to its appeals body.

People argue about the WTO from every direction. Supporters say it kept the world from repeating the 1930s and gave small countries a way to challenge big ones. Critics on one side say it limits a country's freedom to protect its workers and environment. Critics on another side say it does too little about subsidies and unfair practices by large exporters. The standard economic view is that shared rules make trade more predictable, which raises the gains from it, and that the rules should be improved rather than abandoned.

words.d: the international body, founded in 1995, where member countries negotiate trade rules and settle trade disputes
the rule that a country must give every WTO member the same low tariff it gives to any one of them
the WTO process in which panels rule on whether a member has broken trade rules

look.title: A Ruling Nobody Can Enforce
look.text: Country A is found by a WTO panel to have used an illegal subsidy that hurt Country B's aircraft maker. Country A ignores the ruling. Country B is permitted to place tariffs of a set amount on goods from Country A, and it chooses to tax cheese and wine from A's most politically powerful regions.
look.prompt: Why would Country B choose those particular goods? Why might it still prefer that Country A simply comply instead of collecting the tariffs?

check.q: In what year did the WTO replace the GATT as a permanent organization?
check.why: The GATT was signed in 1947 and became the WTO in 1995.

check.q: Under most-favored-nation treatment, a member country must
choices: give its best tariff rate to every other member
charge every country a different tariff
import goods only from its allies
eliminate all tariffs immediately
check.why: MFN means the lowest tariff offered to any member is offered to all of them.

check.q: What can a country do if it wins a WTO dispute and the loser refuses to comply?
choices: Send WTO police to seize goods
Expel the loser from the organization by itself
Nothing at all
Impose retaliatory tariffs of an approved size
check.why: The WTO cannot force compliance, but it authorizes the winner to retaliate with tariffs up to a set amount.

review.q: In one hour Country M makes 8 phones or 4 laptops. Its opportunity cost of one laptop is
choices: 4 phones
2 phones
8 phones
Half a phone
review.why: 4 laptops cost 8 phones, so one laptop costs 2 phones.

review.q: Country M gives up 2 phones per laptop; Country N gives up 1 phone per laptop. Which statement is true?
choices: M should make laptops
N has the absolute advantage in laptops
N has the comparative advantage in laptops
Neither country gains from trade
review.why: N gives up less to make a laptop, so N has the comparative advantage in laptops. Absolute advantage cannot be judged from costs alone.

review.q: A country exports $1,200 billion and imports $1,050 billion. Its trade balance is
choices: a surplus of $150 billion
a deficit of $150 billion
a deficit of $2,250 billion
zero
review.why: Exports minus imports is $1,200 billion minus $1,050 billion, a positive $150 billion surplus.

review.q: Which statement about a U.S. trade deficit is accurate?
choices: It proves foreign countries are cheating
It is the same as the federal budget deficit
It means the country produces nothing
It is matched by foreigners investing in or lending to the United States
review.why: Dollars spent on imports return as purchases of American assets, so a trade deficit pairs with a capital inflow.

review.q: A $400 imported appliance faces a 20% tariff. If the full tariff passes through, what will it cost?
review.why: 20% of $400 is $80, so the price becomes $480.

review.q: Compared with a tariff that raises the price the same amount, a quota
choices: lowers prices for consumers
raises government revenue
sends the price increase to whoever holds import rights
increases the quantity imported
review.why: A quota raises price like a tariff, but the gap between world and domestic price goes to import-right holders, not the treasury.

review.q: Which is the strongest economic objection to a tariff on an intermediate good like steel?
choices: It hurts the many industries that use steel as an input
It makes steel cheaper
It raises no revenue
It has no effect on consumers
review.why: Downstream users of steel employ far more people than steel mills, and their costs rise.

review.q: What does most-favored-nation treatment under the WTO require?
choices: That members trade only with their favorite partner
That members abolish all tariffs
That members charge higher tariffs on rich countries
That members offer every other member their lowest tariff rate
review.why: MFN means the best tariff given to any member must be given to all, with exceptions for free trade areas.
